paragraphs.source_en: At that point, there was no longer any reason to deploy at Hora-ga-tōge. Thus, on the eleventh, Mitsuhide returned once more to Shimo-Toba and redeployed all his forces. paragraphs.source_en: Countless retainers—Hayashi Sado, Sakuma Nobumori, Araki Murashige, and others—had seen their achievements erased by Nobunaga. One might say that Mitsuhide had avenged such men and also relieved the fears of those now serving Nobunaga in constant trepidation, allowing them to govern their domains in peace. Thus, though their outward attitudes remained ambiguous, inwardly they ought to have been profoundly grateful to Mitsuhide.

paragraphs.source_en: Nobunaga, it seemed, had not been the lawless tyrant who made everyone fear for his own safety that Mitsuhide had imagined. Ieyasu, whose own son Nobunaga had forced to death, made no move; nor did the Hosokawa father and son, whom Mitsuhide had firmly believed would ally themselves with him. paragraphs.source_en: Mitsuhide ordered his horse brought, looked up at the sky that had just begun to clear, and climbed a small hill from which Mount Tennō could be plainly seen. Could this little mountain truly decide to whom the realm would ultimately belong? paragraphs.source_en: The gunfire intermingled until friend could no longer be distinguished from foe. Only the battle cries of the two armies could be heard surging toward him like the waves of the sea. The battle gongs of friend and foe rang through one another, while the drums of attack thundered to the heavens. The sight of the two armies grappling in the mire seemed to rise before Mitsuhide's eyes. At this rate, the outcome would be settled before nightfall.
